title: Carrying Uncertainty Without Stalling the Work
summary: Unknowns don't have to stop a project. Name each one specifically, decide whether it blocks, give it an owner and a next check, and decide with open questions on record.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

faqs.q: How do you manage uncertainty on a software project?
faqs.a: Make each unknown specific, decide whether it blocks the work, can travel with it for a while, or is acceptable behind a guardrail, then give it an owner and a dated next check. Review the list regularly. An item that hasn't moved in a week is a signal to ask for help.

faqs.q: What is a spike in software development?
faqs.a: A small, throwaway experiment built to answer one technical question, such as whether a library can handle your load. Extreme Programming describes it as a very simple program to explore potential solutions and expects most spikes to be thrown away.

faqs.q: Should you wait until all uncertainty is gone before deciding?
faqs.a: Usually not. Decide with the open questions written down, put guardrails around the risky ones (a limited rollout, for example), and name the signal that would make you revisit the decision.

html:
"We don't know enough yet." It's often the most honest sentence in a planning meeting, and the one everyone wants to skip past. There's a launch date on the calendar, the design looks nearly done and someone has already started coding. Saying the unknown out loud feels like slowing things down. Pretending it isn't there slows things down more, just later, and usually at a worse moment.

Uncertainty is a normal part of real work. The trouble starts when it stays unnamed, grows in private and finally shows up as rework, a tense argument or a rushed decision nobody is proud of. This post is a small, practical way to keep unknowns visible while the work keeps moving: name them, sort them, give each one an owner and set the next check.

Two sibling posts cover the edges of this. The patience to let context arrive is about when to wait, and reversible decisions are about lowering the stakes of a choice. This one is about the unknowns you have to carry in the meantime.

Why teams hide what they don't know

In Shape Up, Ryan Singer's book on how Basecamp runs projects, work is a hill. "The uphill phase is full of uncertainty, unknowns, and problem solving." The downhill side is execution, when you can see everything and know what to do (Shape Up, Show Progress). A task list can't tell those two phases apart. Ten open tasks might mean ten known steps, or a team that hasn't worked out what the steps are yet.

The same chapter names the human part plainly: "Nobody wants to raise their hand to management and say 'I don't know how to solve this problem.'" And the result: "This causes teams to hide uncertainty and accumulate risk." So the first job is making "I don't know yet" a normal status update, as ordinary as "done" or "in review".

Name it specifically

"This is risky" gives the team nothing to hold on to. Compare:

  • "We don't know whether the old Android client still reads the legacy_price field."
  • "Nobody has measured the partner API's response time under load."
  • "We haven't asked legal whether we can store this data in the EU region."

Each of these has edges. People can see where the unknown starts and stops, and often someone in the room already half-knows the answer. A specific unknown feels smaller than a vague worry, even when it's the same problem underneath.

Decide what kind of unknown it is

Unknowns don't all deserve the same treatment. Roughly three kinds:

  • Blocking: you can't responsibly build further until you know. Resolve it first.
  • Travelling: it can ride along with the work for a while, as long as it has a deadline.
  • Guarded: acceptable once you add a guardrail, like a feature flag, a limit or a fallback.

Treat every unknown as a blocker and the team freezes. Ignore them all and the team gambles. For the planning stage, Shape Up suggests you "walk through a use case in slow motion" looking for holes, then patch the hole, cut that part, or mark it explicitly "out of bounds" (Risks and Rabbit Holes). Out of bounds is an underrated move. Sometimes the cheapest way to resolve an unknown is to decide this version won't handle that case at all.

Give it an owner and a next check

A named unknown with no owner turns into background noise in every meeting. Who will check the logs? Who will confirm the contract with the partner? Who decides whether the answer is good enough? An owner doesn't make the uncertainty go away. It stops it from floating.

Every unknown also needs a next check: a date, a test, a call, a spike, a decision point. Extreme Programming has a name for the technical version. A spike is "a very simple program to explore potential solutions," built to answer one question and usually thrown away afterward (Spike solution). Without a next check, uncertainty spreads across the whole plan. With one, it becomes a task you can track.

A small table in the project doc is enough:

UnknownKindOwnerNext check
Does the old Android client still read legacy_price?BlockingLinhCheck client logs by Wednesday
Partner API latency under loadTravellingMinhLoad test in staging on Friday
Payment postback edge caseGuardedAnKeep rollout at 5% until the postback test passes

Look at it in standup or the weekly sync. If a row hasn't moved in a week, that's your raised hand. Shape Up says the same about its hill charts: "A dot that doesn't move is effectively a raised hand."

Deciding while some questions are still open

Some decisions will still be made with incomplete information. That's normal. What matters is whether the team knows what it's accepting. Compare "we're good to go" with: "We're shipping with the payment postback edge case still open, and we won't widen the rollout past 5% until the postback test passes." The second one still has an open question in it, and anyone reading it knows exactly what to watch.

Unknowns get heavier when you hide them and lighter once they have a shape. Most of the time a specific name, a boundary, an owner and one next check are enough to keep going without pretending you have every answer.

Try this week

  • Pick the vaguest worry on your current project and rewrite it as one specific sentence.
  • Label each open unknown as blocking, travelling or guarded.
  • Give every row an owner and a next-check date.
  • If a case can be declared out of bounds for this version, say so in writing.
